text: Billions of years ago, bacteria faced tiny invaders. Meet the bacteriophage: a virus that injects its DNA into cells.
Bacteria evolved defences. Restriction enzymes act like molecular scissors, cutting invading DNA, while chemical marks help protect their own.
Bacteria also carry plasmids: little rings of DNA that copy themselves. Scientists saw a way to carry new instructions.
In nineteen seventy-three, researchers joined DNA pieces into working plasmids. Bacteria copied them. Nature's tools let us rewrite genetic instructions.
And those instructions could do something amazing. In nineteen seventy-seven, bacteria made a human hormone: tiny cells, working as protein factories.
Human insulin followed, approved in nineteen eighty-two. Purified and tested, it saves lives. Evolution and human curiosity: a remarkable partnership.
